title: BM01: Are You A Super-Connector
author: Richard Claydon
summary: Claydon tells the story of Johan, an ex-submarine commander in IBM Copenhagen's HR department whose unclear job turned out to be making things happen, and uses him to define the 'super-connector'. Super-connectors know what is going on across silos, give without expecting return (drawing on Adam Grant's giver, matcher and taker research), and act as neo-generalists who see connections others miss. His distinctive claim is about sense-making: stories told around the organisation are inevitable data about systemic pain points, and a super-connector maps them before they turn toxic. He argues that KPIs, specialist-and-culture-fit recruitment and machine or culture views of organisation undervalue these people, who also keep strong cultures from becoming closed systems and make specialists more useful. The essay closes with a call to find and hire super-connectors, with the personal anecdote carrying most of the evidence rather than data.
points: A super-connector links people across silos, gives freely, and creates value by drawing together information others cannot see.
Using Adam Grant's findings, givers can look like low performers by KPI, yet removing them degrades collaboration across the whole organisation.
Claydon treats workplace stories as sensors: a super-connector maps patterns in them to find systemic causes before they become toxic.
KPIs, specialist hiring and culture-fit screening cannot see this value, so organisations tend to expel or never hire these people.
Super-connectors guard strong cultures against groupthink by surfacing employees' outside interests and making specialists legible to others.
quotes: Super-connectors are the people in organisations who know what is going on everywhere. They pay no attention to silos, crossing domain boundaries with ease and dexterity. Well-liked and well-informed, they are the people you turn to for help when some intractably wicked problems start causing you headaches.
Super-connectors might not know how to help you. But they’ll damn sure connect you with people who can.

While some givers go on to be the highest performing people in all the organisations Grant has examined (and it’s a lot!), other givers actually don’t do very well in organisational life. Indeed, they are perceived as the lowest performers.

If you get rid of your super-connectors, even the “low performing ones”, the glue of giving without expectation stops sticking things together. Over time, the organisation suffers, potentially catastrophically, as all efforts for collaboration, vital in today’s complex working environment, get undermined by organisational terrorists.

Much organisational culture thinking today starts from the assumption that these stories are bad and can be eliminated by hiring the right people for the company. They are not bad. They are inevitable.

In today’s interconnected complexity of work, it is next to impossible to isolate performance to the granular, individualised level of a KPI. Everything happens in dynamic context, impacting and being impacted by stuff that is going on elsewhere. A super-connector navigates this complexity for the benefit of all.

In doing the above, they make specialists more valuable. A specialist who has no concept of how his work gets interpreted beyond his specialism can produce outputs that look completely stupid to the wider world.
